text.p: Diversified technology company Sulzer AG on Tuesday said 1997 would bring a return to rising profits after two years of sharp declines that have prompted major restructuring in the group.

Sulzer said it had settled its biggest financial problems with two steps last year -- deciding to cut jobs and production at loss-making weaving machinery division Sulzer Rueti and paying damages in a U.S. patent dispute.
Sulzer, which saw net profit plunge 53 percent in 1995 due to one-off costs and lower earnings in most divisions, posted an 11 percent drop in 1996 to 82 million Swiss francs.
"The group is at a turning point. We are on our way back up," chairman Pierre Borgeaud told a news conference on 1996 results.
Borgeud said one key factor in the turnaround was a strategic decision in January to spin off medical technology division Sulzer Medica this year and put a quarter of its equity on the market.

Sulzer AG will then become a holding for Medica and an industrial side made up of Sulzer Infra (plant and building services), Sulzer Winterthur (locomotives, turbines), Sulzer Roteq (pumps, compressors) as well as Rueti.
Sulzer blamed last year's renewed profit slump on three main factors.

One was a loss of 97 million Swiss francs at Sulzer Rueti, including 56 million francs for slashing jobs and closing one of two Swiss plants in a reorganisation aimed at regaining profitabilty despite a shrinking world market for weaving machines.

Another factor was a U.S. court ruling in a a patent case against a subsidiary of Medica that cost the Swiss group 73 million Swiss francs, cutting 1996 operating profit at Sulzer's most profitable division by 21 percent to 151 million.

In addition, Sulzer said building services unit Sulzer Infra was still suffering from a construction slump in its main European markets, although it had trimmed operating losses by 45 percent from 1995 to 29 million Swiss francs last year.
Chief executive Fritz Fahrni said the year had started well and the group expected "a strong increase in both net and operating profits".
"New orders in the first two months were a pleasing nine percent higher than in the comparative period," Fahrni said.

Fahrni told the news conference Sulzer would still need around 20 to 30 million Swiss francs a year for ongoing restructuring as it adapts to market demands and continues a policy of smaller acquisitions and divestitures.
Fahrni said Sulzer expected to achieve a return on equity (ROE) of 14 percent for its industrial business and 17 percent at Sulzer Medica in three to four years.
ROE for the Medica unit was 10.6 percent in 1996. For the industrial operations, ROE was minus 1.8 percent due mainly to the losses at Rueti and Infra last year.
